Table 28 lists "3.5 inch (x12) SAS/SATA backplane" on its own as a supported option, and this is it: twelve 3.5 inch carriers in 3 rows of 4, over the three-riser rear. ONLY THE BAYS DIFFER FROM THE 24-BAY FRONT. ISM table 2 lists the same four features on both fronts - left control panel, drive slots, right control panel, information tag - so the panels, the latches, the bezel and every port on the right are shared, and the drive field is the same backplane opening divided four ways instead of twenty-four.","kind":"orderable","skins":{"db9":"teal"},"views":{"front":"front-lff-12"}},"lff-12-rear-2-lff":{"description":"THE PAIRING TABLE 28 ACTUALLY LISTS: "3.5 inch (x12) SAS/SATA backplane and 3.5 inch (x2) SAS/SATA backplane (back)". That configuration records, in its own description, that no row of table 28 pairs a 24 x 2.5 inch front with a 2 x 3.5 inch rear, and that it was therefore a picture of a rear rather than of a machine. IT HAD NO CONFIGURATION UNTIL NOW and the variant sheet reported that as a gap: it is the only row in table 25 that fits riser 2 without riser 3, so nothing in the device named it and the drawing could only be produced by overriding a bay from outside.","kind":"orderable","skins":{"db9":"teal","pcie-slot-strip-14g":"no-2"}},"rear-2-lff":{"description":"DRAWN NOW, AND IT IS A PICTURE OF A REAR RATHER THAN OF A MACHINE. common/drive-carrier-35 exists, measured off ISM figure 9, so the two 3.5 inch bays and the numbering on the divider between them are real and sourced. What is not real is the pairing: table 28 has no row with a 24 x 2.5 inch front and a 2 x 3.5 inch rear, so selecting this shows a correct rear on a front it never ships with. THE ID CLASH IS THAT MISMATCH MADE VISIBLE. The figure prints 12 and 13, which are already two of this chassis's front bays, so the rear ones are rear-drive-12 and rear-drive-13 rather than following the ink the way drive-24 to drive-27 do. Named the obvious way, lint caught full-24 fitting a 2.5 inch carrier into a 3.5 inch bay. It stops being an illustration the day the 12 x 3.5 inch front is drawn and a configuration binds the two faces together.","kind":"example","skins":{"db9":"teal"}},"rear-4-sff":{"bays":{"drive-24":"common/drive-carrier-25@1","drive-25":"common/drive-carrier-25@1","drive-26":"common/drive-carrier-25@1","drive-27":"common/drive-carrier-25@1"},"description":"four 2.5 inch drives in the rear, which costs riser 2's two full-height slots and all of riser 3 - the R740xd ISM figure 8. ISM table 25 names riser configurations 0, 1 and 2 that way - one riser layout, two storage outcomes - and every other configuration on this device draws the "with". Here the one-slot low-profile riser 2 is fitted, no drives were ordered, and both rear bays carry a perforated blank. IT IS ORDERABLE WHERE rear-2-lff IS NOT. Table 28's rows 1, 3 and 9 all pair a 24 x 2.5 inch front with no rear backplane at all, which is exactly this machine, so unlike the 2 x 3.5 inch illustration this is a build you can buy. WHAT IT DOES NOT SHOW is riser 3: configurations 1 and 2 fit none, and the bay it would occupy is the one blanked here. `no-rear-storage` is the other shape - a three-slot riser 2 and a riser 3 - and the two are not the same machine despite both having no rear drives.","kind":"orderable","skins":{"db9":"teal","rear-bay-screw-tab-14g":"pad-only"}}},"description":"2U two-socket rack server - 24 x 2.5 inch front drive bays","format":1,"gaps":[{"note":"ISM table 28 puts a MID DRIVE TRAY in three of its ten backplane rows - 2.5 inch x4 behind the 24-bay front, 3.5 inch x4 behind the 12-bay one. This device models no mid bay at all, so a third of the orderable combinations cannot be expressed and a whole drive location is absent. IT IS NOT A FACE. The tray sits under the lid between the fans and the backplane, so it belongs to a top view with the cover off, which this device does not have either. Recorded here because a reader counting drive bays against a spec sheet will find this device short and no view will explain why. IT IS NO LONGER SHORT OF NUMBERS. Dell's own R740XD 3D guide CAD carries `740XD_ MidDriveTray_-1.001` at 431.5 x 94.5 x 181.2 mm, with its bracket (`740XD_ MidDriveTray_ Bracket-1.001`, 73.40 x 18.10 x 117.00) and its drives (`740XD_ MidDriveTray_ 2.5 HDD-5.002`, 69.90 x 15.00 x 100.20 on a 108.4 pitch) as named sub-parts. The R740 and R740xd Technical Guide adds what the tray is FOR - "The 4 x 3.5-inch mid-bay storage option, which also supports 2.5-inch drives in the Hybrid carrier" - which also names the hybrid carrier this library does not have. An interior photograph is staged beside the front one in working/intake/dell/r740xd/photos. So what remains is drawing, not measuring.","reason":"needs-drawing","scope":["front","rear"],"wanted":"A top-with-cover-off view and a mid-tray bay group, or an explicit statement that this library models only externally visible bays. Either answers the question; leaving it unsaid does not. The geometry is now available from the CAD rather than needing to be estimated.","what":"mid-drive-tray"},{"note":"ISM figures 17 and 18 number five fronts - 24, 16 and 8 x 2.5 inch at bays 0-23, 0-15 and 0-7, and 12 and 8 x 3.5 inch at 0-11 and 0-7. TWO OF THE FIVE ARE NOW DRAWN. `front` is the 24 x 2.5 inch; `front-lff-12` is the 12 x 3.5 inch, the one that mattered, because it is the front the rears numbered 12-15 and 12-13 belong to. It is a variant view with `face: front`, bound by `lff-12` and `lff-12-rear-2-lff`, and its grid was measured off dellr740xd-12x35.webp at Gate 1 0.07% - the same backplane opening the 24 SFF bays divide, 428.832 / 4 = 107.208 against a measured period of 107.216. THE 16 AND 8 x 2.5 INCH AND THE 8 x 3.5 INCH ARE STILL NOT MODELLED, and no figure for them has been measured.","reason":"needs-drawing","scope":["front","front-lff-12"],"wanted":"the remaining three fronts as further `face: front` variants, each with a configuration to bind it.","what":"front-panel-variants"},{"note":"DELL ENUMERATES THEM. ISM table 28, "Supported backplane options for PowerEdge R740XD systems", lists front, mid and rear together - ten rows, and the coupling falls straight out:
 2.5in x24 no rear
 2.5in x24 + 2.5in x4 mid + 2.5in x4 rear
 2.5in x24 (20 SAS/SATA + 4 NVMe) no rear
 3.5in x12 no rear
 3.5in x12 + 3.5in x4 mid + 3.5in x2 rear
 3.5in x12 + 3.5in x4 mid + 2.5in x4 rear
 3.5in x12 + 3.5in x2 rear
 3.5in x12 + 2.5in x4 rear
 2.5in x24 NVMe no rear
 3.5in x12 Hybrid with NVMe U.2 no rear
The 24-bay front takes ONE rear, the 4 x 2.5 inch, which figure 19 numbers 24-27. The 12-bay front takes either, and figure 19 numbers both from 12. This device carries the 24-bay front, which is why its rear reads 24-27. THE ARITHMETIC GOT THERE FIRST AND IS NOW REDUNDANT. Bays numbered 12-15 imply eleven bays this model does not have; that is how the error was found. Table 28 is how it is now SOURCED, and a guess agreeing with a document afterwards is worth more than either alone. THE RISER SIDE IS TABLE 25, and its discriminator is riser 2 rather than riser 3. Rear storage is offered in riser configurations 0, 1 and 2 and no others: 1 and 2 fit a one-slot low-profile riser 2 (2B or 2C, slot 4 only), while configuration 3 fits a three-slot 2A (slots 4, 5, 6) and has NO rear storage despite fitting no riser 3 at all. It is riser 2's full-height section that occupies the bay the rear cage needs. This device's `no-rear-storage` and `rear-4-sff` already encode exactly that, and row 3 itself is now `no-riser-3` - added when the riser 3 opening and rear storage bay 3 turned out to be the SAME HOLE, closed by two different blanks depending on which configuration you picked. RE-READ AND STILL OPEN: that change touched which bay closes an opening, not the front-to-rear coupling this gap is about. Re-read again when riser 1's brackets moved 1 mm and slot 2 lost its numeral on 1A - both are ink and geometry inside one bay, and neither reaches across faces. Re-read a third time when riser 1's plate grew to meet the slot strip and the shroud: the bay's own box moved, and still nothing crossed a face. A fourth time when riser 2's three slots were aligned and its plate cut back to the full-height pair. That one surfaced a NEW question but not a new gap of this kind: a bay's occupant is drawn after the panel, so a card cannot be shown "only through its cutout" without a part drawn after the bays to mask it. Recorded where it belongs, on the riser 2 slot 6 cutout, rather than widened into this one. A fifth time when the screw tab was split out of the frame so it could draw in front of riser 2's bracket tails. That is a draw-order fact about one bay, not a coupling between faces. A sixth time when riser 3 became bay 1 reflected - mirrored brackets, a two-slot plate and its own slot strip. Handedness is a fact about one bay's own metal and reaches no further than that. A seventh time when riser 3 slid 9.525 right to sit over the power supply's edge. Moving one bay along its own face changes nothing about which front it can be sold with. An eighth time when two "rivet" pairs beside the divider turned out to be card retention clips. A misread of what is on the rear, corrected on the rear, and silent about any front. A ninth time when those rivets came back, scoped: they are what the riser cage mounts to and they show when drives are fitted instead. That one is a rear configuration telling two rear drawings apart, which is the mechanism this gap says is MISSING between faces - and still is. A tenth time when the C20 supply became its own part. A second occupant for an existing bay, on the same face, coupled to nothing at the front. TWO SOURCES DISAGREE AND ARE LEFT DISAGREEING. The system information label draws FIVE fronts - 24, 16 and 8 x 2.5 inch, 12 and 8 x 3.5 inch - where table 28 lists TWO front backplanes. Whether the 16- and 8-bay fronts are different chassis or one backplane drawn part-populated, nothing held here says. AND TABLE 28 HAS A MID DRIVE TRAY in three of its ten rows. This device models no mid bay at all, which is a whole third drive location missing rather than a detail.","reason":"vendor-silent","scope":["front","front-lff-12","rear","rear-4-sff","rear-2-lff","lff-12","lff-12-rear-2-lff"],"wanted":"NOW DEMONSTRABLE RATHER THAN HYPOTHETICAL. `rear-2-lff` draws a correct 2 x 3.5 inch rear on a 24 x 2.5 inch front, and ISM table 28 lists no such machine - every row carrying that rear has a 12-bay front. The mismatch even forced an id: the figure prints 12 and 13, which are already two of this chassis's front bays, so the rear ones had to be rear-drive-12 and rear-drive-13. An id clash is what this gap looks like from the inside. RE-READ AFTER THE REAR BAYS WERE SEPARATED, and still open. The rear half of this is now expressible: the chassis structure across bays 2 and 3 is its own always-present part, and what each bay holds - drives, PCIe, a blank - varies independently of the other. That was the piece `only-in` could not reach while one 287 mm component owned both bays. WHAT REMAINS IS THE FRONT. The 24 x 2.5 inch and 12 x 3.5 inch fronts are different panels, not different occupancy, and until the second is drawn nothing exercises the face-binding that would couple it to a rear. A way for a configuration to constrain more than one view at once. Today `only-in` scopes a bay to a configuration and every view chooses independently, so nothing stops a consumer selecting a 24-bay front and a rear numbered 12-15 - a machine that cannot be bought. The library needs either configurations that span views, or a declared incompatibility between them; and this device needs its 12 x 3.5 inch front modelled before either can be exercised, which is the same gap `rear-2-lff` already stands on.","what":"front-rear-configuration-coupling"},{"note":"THE MISSING THING IS A DECISION, NOT EVIDENCE, and `reason` has no token for that - `needs-drawing` is the nearest, because one of the two ways out is a second rear panel. The vendor is not silent and the sources do not disagree; the model cannot say it. TABLE 28 LISTS "3.5 inch (x12) ... and 2.5 inch (x4) SAS/SATA backplane (back)" AND IT CANNOT BE SPELLED HERE. The four rear 2.5 inch bays are `drive-24..27`, and those ids ARE the 24-bay front's numbering; under the 12 x 3.5 inch front the same four bays are drives 12-15. A bay id does not vary by configuration, so one set of bays cannot carry both numberings, and `configurations.<name>.views` does not reach it - that couples which PANEL a face wears, not what the bays on another face are called. `rear-2-lff` escaped this only by accident of naming: its bays were already `rear-drive-12` and `rear-drive-13`, so `lff-12-rear-2-lff` binds them without contradiction. THIS IS THE RESIDUE OF "the two rear numberings stop being mutually exclusive readings of one drawing", and drawing the front did not settle it - it made it precise.","reason":"needs-drawing","scope":["front-lff-12","rear-4-sff"],"wanted":"a decision on how a bay carries a per-configuration label: either a second rear variant view whose bays are named for the LFF numbering, which duplicates a panel to rename four bays, or a `labels:` override in the configuration, which is new schema.","what":"lff-front-rear-4-sff-numbering"}],"groups":{"covers":{"description":"removable covers over the face. The bezel is the only one, and it is drawn only when asked for: it hides the drives it protects, which is the whole point of it and exactly why the default drawing leaves it off.","index-origin":1,"role":"service","term":"Cover"},"drives":{"attrs":{"media":"sff-2.5"},"description":"the 24 front bays. `service` rather than `traffic` because the five roles are network-shaped and traffic means a revenue port; a drive is a field-replaceable module that does the machine's work, which is the nearest of the five and is said here rather than left to be guessed.","index-origin":0,"role":"service","term":"Drive"},"drives-rear":{"attrs":{"media":"sff-2.5"},"description":"the rear drive bays, which exist only on a rear-storage chassis. DELL NUMBERS THEM 12 TO 15, continuing the front row rather than starting again, and that numbering is carried in each bay's `rel-pos`; `index-origin` takes only 0 or 1 so it cannot express a run beginning at 12, and it is left at 0 rather than made to lie.","index-origin":0,"role":"service","term":"Drive"},"furniture":{"description":"removable ironmongery that is neither a port nor a lamp. The rear handle is the only one: the ISM says it comes off to let cables out of PCIe slot 6, but gives it no removal procedure of its own, so it is documented as removable without being a serviceable unit.","index-origin":1,"role":"furniture","term":"Item"},"latches":{"description":"the rack release rockers, one built into each ear. Pressed to free the chassis from the rail so it can be drawn out - so they are pressed, but they release the BOX rather than operating anything in it, which is why they are furniture and not `mgmt`.","index-origin":1,"role":"furniture","term":"Latch"},"leds":{"description":"indicators that are not part of a control panel module. Only one on this face: the iDRAC Direct lamp under its port.","index-origin":1,"role":"indicator","term":"LED"},"marks":{"description":"printed and moulded marks that say what the opening beside them is for. They are `furniture` because nothing plugs into them and nothing lights - a mark that lit would be a lamp, and this panel has one of those and it is the power button.","index-origin":1,"role":"furniture","term":"Mark"},"mgmt":{"description":"the power button - what you press, not what you plug into","index-origin":1,"role":"management","term":"Control"},"mgmt-ports":{"description":"the rear I/O: iDRAC9 dedicated, serial, VGA and two USB 3.0. Four families in one block deliberately, the same reason as the front - Dell's table calls them one panel and they do one job.","index-origin":1,"mixed":"rear service access","role":"management","term":"Port"},"mgmt-rear":{"description":"the rear system identification button - what you press, not what you plug into, which is why it is not in `mgmt-ports` with the sockets.","index-origin":1,"role":"management","term":"Control"},"ndc":{"description":"the network daughter card slot, and the only fixed NIC this chassis has. THE GROUP HOLDS THE CARD, NOT ITS PORTS, and that is why it is `service` rather than `traffic`. The four RJ45s are elements of the part and they do carry traffic; the SLOT is standard equipment that ships filled, in the way a supervisory engine does, rather than an expansion choice a buyer makes. A base configuration is a chassis you can log into with nothing decided about expansion - and it cannot be logged into over a NIC that the base left out.","index-origin":1,"role":"service","term":"Card"},"panels":{"description":"the control panels, which are field-replaceable units rather than features of the metal - the ISM carries removal and installation procedures for each. The right-hand one is still drawn as loose placements and is the next thing to become a module.","index-origin":1,"role":"service","term":"Panel"},"ports":{"description":"the front I/O: two USB 2.0, the iDRAC Direct micro USB and the VGA. Three families in one block DELIBERATELY - Dell's own table calls them one thing, the right control panel, and they do one job: they are what you plug a keyboard, a screen and a laptop into when you are standing at the rack. Splitting them by media would draw three groups where the faceplate has one. None of them is traffic; this chassis carries no network port on its front face.","index-origin":1,"mixed":"local console and service access","role":"management","term":"Port"},"psus":{"attrs":{"redundancy":"1+1","redundancy-note":"1+1 - Dell R740xd Installation and Service Manual: "When two identical PSUs are installed, power supply redundancy (1+1 - with redundancy or 2+0 - without redundancy) is configured in system BIOS." The pair is 1+1 by default and the same two supplies can be set to 2+0, which is the vendor offering the choice rather than a second product. Hot spare puts the redundant PSU to sleep while the active one carries 100 percent of the load"},"index-origin":1,"role":"service","term":"PSU"},"risers":{"description":"the three expansion card riser positions. `service` AND NOT `traffic`, which is the same distinction the NDC group makes: the group holds the RISER, and a riser is infrastructure that ships fitted. The traffic choice is the CARD, and cards live in the riser's own nested bays - so a base configuration seats risers without deciding anything about expansion, exactly as it should. THE SLOTS ARE NOT IN THIS GROUP because they are not on the chassis: each riser carries its own bays, so a slot is numbered within its riser and the riser is numbered within the chassis. That nesting is what lets the same low-profile opening be slot 4 under one riser and slot 6 under another.","index-origin":1,"role":"service","term":"Riser"}},"kind":"device","manufacturer":"Dell","maturity":"draft","model":"PowerEdge R740xd","name":"r740xd","profile":"server","provenance":{"bay-origin":"THE ARRAY IS CENTRED, and that is a measurement rather than an assumption. ISM figure 2 puts the first release ring 35.27 mm from the left edge of the face and the last at 447.18, so the array runs 26.3..456.1 and leaves margins of 26.3 and 26.5 - symmetric to 0.15 mm. Implausibility is a failed check; symmetry here is the check passing. x is therefore (482.6 - 24 x 17.868)/2 = 26.884.","bay-pitch":"17.868 mm, read three times from three documents that agree to 0.05 mm: Dell's marketing render of this device (Gate 1 2.10%) gives 17.868; the r750-24d-2-5-front Visio master, a line drawing of the 15G successor that passes Gate 1 at 0.67%, gives 17.8454 across 23 gaps of exact vector coordinates; and ISM figure 2 at 600 dpi gives 17.9094 from the 24 orange release rings. The device's OWN source is kept - adopting a measurement of a different machine would trade provenance for false precision - and the other two are corroboration.","bay-vertical":"drawing - the r750 master draws 22 of its 24 carriers with an identical outline at y 4.01..83.02, height 79.01 mm (bays 1 and 24 catch chassis paths and are excluded). Correcting the 0.7% by which that master draws the face 87.39 mm tall instead of 86.8 gives 78.48. common/drive-carrier-25 carries 79.4 from an independent source, and 0.5% agreement between a render and a line drawing is why that figure stands rather than being re-derived here.","bezel":"DRAWN FITTED, AND IT DECLARES WHAT IT HIDES. `for:` names all 24 drive bays and the left control panel, which is how the C40G's snap-on PSU cover says it sits over four supplies - the same construction, and the reason L13 does not read a cover as a sizing mistake. A viewer can then hide it and see what is behind, which is the point. An earlier draft made it an `optional:` placement, the mechanism the SmartOptics rack ears use, and that was the wrong tool: `optional:` is for something absent unless asked for, and this is something PRESENT that a reader chooses to look past. IT CLEARS BOTH EARS AND DOES NOT COVER THE WHOLE FACE. At 434 x 82.35 centred on the 482.6 x 86.8 face it leaves 24.3 mm of ear showing each side and 2.2 above and below, which is the operator's description of where it sits and is what fixed its size - see dell/bezel-2u-14g, whose master aspect fails Gate 1 against a rack face precisely because a rack face is not what it covers.","chassis":"datasheet - the R740xd spec sheet gives Height 86.8 mm, Width 434 mm, Depth 737.5 mm and notes the figures exclude the bezel. 434 is the BODY between the ear folds; the drawn front face is 482.6 because this device's ears carry ports (see front-face).","drive-default":"EVERY BAY DEFAULTS TO A BLANK. A bay with nothing in it renders as an open hole, and a rack server does not ship with 24 open holes - it ships filled, because the airflow depends on it. Dell publishes no default drive count for this chassis, so the honest default is the filler rather than a drive count somebody invented. A populated machine is a configuration.","front-face":"THE EARS ARE PART OF THE FACEPLATE AND CARRY PORTS, so they are drawn. Dell builds the mounting flanges into the front moulding and puts the VGA in the right-hand ear, the power button and USB stack in the strip beside it, and the system health lamp in the left. A 434 mm face would leave real, field-visible ports with nowhere to live. L43 tests what is seated in the outer 25 mm rather than the width, and passes this device for that reason.","gate-1":"ISM figure 2 'Front view of 24 x 2.5 inch drive system', rendered from the PDF at 600 dpi, measures 3168 x 564 px on the chassis itself - aspect 5.6170 against 482.6/86.8 = 5.5599, which is 1.03%. ORTHOGRAPHIC, and at 6.5644 px/mm. That distinction is the document's own and it is worth spelling out, because two other glyph columns on this chassis work the other way: the drive carrier's head glyphs ARE its lamps and the left panel's five status glyphs ARE its lamps. Here ISM table 7 lists the iDRAC Direct PORT as item 3 with a wrench icon and the iDRAC Direct LED as item 4 with `Icon: N/A`, and figure 7's callout for item 4 points below the socket at plain strip. The wrench marks the hole; the lamp beneath it carries no mark at all. ITS CODES ARE SOURCED AND ITS PLACE IS APPROXIMATE, and those are not the same confidence. Table 8 gives all three codes. For the position the ISM says only "located below the iDRAC Direct port on the right control panel" and figure 7's callout agrees with that much; figure 2 at 6.5644 px/mm resolves the socket and the wrench above it and shows nothing beneath them, and figure 7 is schematic and carries no scale. So the 2.5 mm offset here is a sentence turned into a coordinate, and the size is common/led-dot's 2 mm, which that part itself calls estimated.","left-control-panel":"photo-measured from ISM figure 2 at 6.5644 px/mm. NOT taken from the R750 master, which disagrees by 1.9 mm in x on the light bar and so is a different panel - the agreement that licensed the right-hand panel does not hold here, and reading it across anyway would have been the same evidence used twice with the negative result discarded.","not-yet-modelled":"THIS IS A FRONT-FACE DRAFT AND SAYS SO. The r750 master draws the same 12.16 x 37.99 section at x 2.80 and x 469.04, both starting at y 46.91 - 54% down an 86.8 face - and the operator describes the hardware the same way, "a little bit lower than midway down, and from there to the bottom". A drawing of the successor and a machine in a rack agreeing on where a feature starts is what fixed it. THE LEFT ONE IS CENTRED ON ITS EAR AND NOT ON THE MASTER'S x. The r750 draws it at x 2.80 in an ear of its own width; this chassis's left ear is 13.41 wide, so 2.80 put a 12.16 part 2.2 mm off centre and 1.55 mm past the ear's edge. A position read from another machine's drawing has to be re-seated against the metal it lands on - the master gives the part's SIZE, and the ear it sits in gives its PLACE. The right-hand one needed no such move: its ear runs 468.54..482.6 and the master's 469.04 already centres it there. An earlier reading took the right-hand one for the information tag. The Information Update tech sheet's table 3 enumerates TWELVE riser configurations - 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 9, 15, 16 and 17 - each naming which slots exist on risers 1, 2 and 3 and at what height and length: riser configuration 0 has no PCIe slots at all and only rear storage, 1 and 2 give four slots with or without it, 4 and 5 and 15 give eight. WHAT IS DRAWN HERE IS THE SHAPE OF THE ANSWER, not the whole of it. The three configurations modelled - no rear storage, four 2.5 inch rear, two 3.5 inch rear - establish that competing slot sets and drive bays are METAL scoped by `only-in` rather than different occupants of one hole. Every occurrence of "blink" in this device's manual belongs to some other lamp - the health bar, Quick Sync, the NIC indicators or a PSU handle. g.data-description: the power button - what you press, not what you plug into
g.title: power-btn

g.data-description: the power symbol itself, lit from behind. It is the glyph that lights, not a separate indicator beside it, which is why the element is the symbol's own box rather than a dot.

the front I/O: two USB 2.0, the iDRAC Direct micro USB and the VGA. Three families in one block DELIBERATELY - Dell's own table calls them one thing, the right control panel, and they do one job: they are what you plug a keyboard, a screen and a laptop into when you are standing at the rack. Splitting them by media would draw three groups where the faceplate has one. None of them is traffic; this chassis carries no network port on its front face.
g.title: usb-1

g.data-description: printed and moulded marks that say what the opening beside them is for. They are `furniture` because nothing plugs into them and nothing lights - a mark that lit would be a lamp, and this panel has one of those and it is the power button.
g.title: mark-usb-1

g.title: panel-grid

g.data-description: ISM table 8 entire. `connected` is "solid green for two seconds" - a laptop or tablet has been plugged in, and the two seconds is how long that indication lasts before the next one rather than a blink, so it is modelled solid and the duration recorded here instead of being invented as a rate. `recognised` is "flashing green (on for two seconds and off for two seconds)", which is 0.25 Hz exactly. `off` is the device unplugged.
g.title: idrac-direct-led

g.data-description: the rack release rockers, one built into each ear. Pressed to free the chassis from the rail so it can be drawn out - so they are pressed, but they release the BOX rather than operating anything in it, which is why they are furniture and not `mgmt`.
g.title: latch-left

rect.data-description: the pressed face at the top of the rocker, where the finger goes. Below it the moulding is a plain grip.

g.data-description: the rack release rockers, one built into each ear. Pressed to free the chassis from the rail so it can be drawn out - so they are pressed, but they release the BOX rather than operating anything in it, which is why they are furniture and not `mgmt`.
g.title: latch-right

rect.data-description: the pressed face at the top of the rocker, where the finger goes. Below it the moulding is a plain grip.

g.data-description: the drive glyph, lit. ISM table 4 - solid amber if there is a drive error.
the thermometer glyph. Solid amber on a thermal error - ambient out of range, or a fan failure.
the lightning glyph. Solid amber on voltage out of range, a failed PSU or a failed voltage regulator.
the memory glyph. Solid amber on a memory error.
the PCIe glyph. Solid amber when a PCIe card errors.

rect.data-description: the system health and system ID bar, and the button that switches between the two modes. ISM table 5 in full: solid blue - on, healthy, ID mode not active; blinking blue - ID mode active; solid amber - fail-safe mode; blinking amber - a fault, check the event log. NO RATE IS PUBLISHED for either blink, so 1 Hz is this library's reading and is not a figure Dell states - unlike the drive lamp, where the article gives twice and four times a second and the model carries them.

rect.data-states: off ready transfer updating disabled fail-safe unresponsive
rect.data-description: the iDRAC Quick Sync 2 bar, and the button that turns the feature on and off. Every code in ISM table 6, at the shape that table gives. `disabled` IS WHY THE SEQUENCE MECHANISM EXISTS: Dell's wording is 'blinks white five times rapidly and then turns off', which is five on-phases, five off-phases and a long dark tail - a pattern no colour and rate can say. The 2.5 second tail is this library's reading of 'and then turns off'; the five blinks are Dell's own count.
